title: A Preregistered Audit of Dataset Contamination Controls in LLM-for-NetOps Benchmarks
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired, confirmatory audit measuring whether conservative, deterministic contamination detectors (exact-match + fuzzy 5‑gram + provenance heuristics) flag items in a sampled set of NetOps tasks and whether applying preregistered contamination controls changes validator‑based success rates. Under a frozen plan (study contamination-audit-netops-2026-v1) we evaluated 150 item pairs (baseline vs guarded) with a single hosted model (declared_model_version = gpt-5-mini) using a deterministic generate–validate procedure and a formal netops validator. Preregistered detectors produced zero high‑confidence contamination flags for the executed items; accordingly no guarded exclusions/replacements occurred. All 150 baseline episodes and their matched guarded episodes passed the validator (baseline = 150/150, guarded = 150/150). The preregistered paired test yields paired_success_rate_difference = 0.0 percentage points (95% CI [0.0, 0.0]), exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. We report this artifact‑backed null, reconcile a preregistration→analysis hypothesis identifier mapping, explicitly document that the executed sample used deterministically generated synthetic tasks (source_identifier prefix "synthetic-netops:"), and discuss how preregistered generation semantics limited sensitivity. We provide artifact pointers to the archived execution and analysis records so readers can verify the reported numbers.

sections.introduction: Generative large language models (LLMs) are increasingly proposed to translate high‑level intent into concrete NetOps artifacts (device configurations, automated repairs). Reliable operational adoption requires not only capable models but also evaluation integrity: benchmark contamination (memorized items) and construct invalidity (templated tasks) can inflate measured success. Motivated by methodological critiques of LLM evaluation and by recent LLM‑for‑NetOps benchmarks, we preregistered an audit to (a) measure the prevalence of preregistered, conservative contamination flags in a deterministically sampled set of NetOps items, and (b) measure how much applying those preregistered contamination controls (exclude high‑confidence flags and deterministically replace them) changes validator‑based success rates. Research question: After freezing a deterministic contamination‑detection and realism‑adjustment protocol, how many high‑confidence contamination flags occur in a reproducible 150‑item sample, and how much does applying the preregistered controls change the model's validator pass rate? Contributions: (1) a fully preregistered, artifact‑backed paired confirmatory experiment (study id contamination-audit-netops-2026-v1); (2) exact, archived confirmatory statistics on Npairs = 150 with deterministic validator traces; (3) a diagnostic reconciliation explaining the observed null outcome and prescriptive recommendations for stronger future audits.
sections.related_work: Prior system and benchmark work shows that LLMs can produce plausible configuration artifacts under constrained settings but often introduce regressions unless paired with verification or iterative repair loops; agentic integrations with external validators reduce regressions on average but do not eliminate per‑case failures [arXiv:2604.22513; arXiv:2606.06212]. Deterministic network verification tools (header‑space style analyzers and NetKAT/NetPlumber families) are standard oracles for reachability and policy properties and motivate using a formal validator as the episode pass/fail oracle [Kazemian et al.; Beckett et al.]. Methodological studies of LLM evaluation document contamination and construct‑validity risks and recommend provenance‑aware detection, thresholded n‑gram overlap, and human adjudication for borderline cases; our audit operationalizes a conservative subset of those recommendations in a preregistered generate–validate design [evaluation surveys].
sections.methodology: Preregistration and estimand — We froze the plan described in preregistration study contamination-audit-netops-2026-v1. The preregistration specified the primary confirmatory estimand as the paired success‑rate difference (paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline; preregistered primary hypothesis label H2) to be tested by the paired_binary_analysis_v1 executor. During analysis the confirmatory result record appears under hypothesis_id 'H1'; we explicitly map that analysis record to the preregistered primary hypothesis label H2 here and cite the authoritative analysis input artifact (input_results_sha256 = 5337998d1d86aca507f77659d75cc9487cf3d87a157ed5044b8a9d5ff79b5586) so the mapping is verifiable. Sampling, generation, and replacement rules — The preregistration listed a public benchmark_scope but also prespecified deterministic replacement rules for excluded/unavailable items. The executed sampling used a deterministic task generator (deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5) that produced provenance‑normalized, reproducible synthetic items; the execution task manifest records the executed sample and per‑task source identifiers (entries use source_identifier values with prefix "synthetic-netops:"). The execution task manifest path is execution/task_manifest.jsonl and its recorded SHA‑256 is b7c08599e3f96d8d5605a18f8f973e0707d7224327eeed7bde78c0d34cb83e55 (see archived execution bundle). We therefore reconcile the preregistered benchmark_scope with the executed sample as follows: the preregistration allowed deterministic replacements; for this run replacement was performed via the preregistered deterministic task generator to produce provenance‑stable synthetic items for the 150‑item confirmatory sample (the execution manifest contains the per‑task source_identifier fields showing this). Contamination detectors and guarded treatment — The preregistered detectors were (1) exact normalized‑token equality, (2) fuzzy 5‑gram overlap (shingle Jaccard/overlap) with high‑confidence threshold overlap ≥ 0.80, and (3) provenance timestamp heuristics vs model cutoff. The preregistered guarded treatment excluded high‑confidence flagged items and deterministically replaced them with retemplated + topology‑augmented items preserving intent (per preregistration rules). In the executed sample no items met the preregistered high‑confidence flag criteria and thus no replacements were applied (see analysis/contamination_summary.csv below). Generation semantics and validator — The preregistration specified shared_initial_candidate semantics across conditions (independent_condition_generation = false) to reduce model‑call variance; execution honored that choice. Model configuration and provider accounting are recorded in execution/model_configuration.json (declared_model_version = "gpt-5-mini"); the model configuration artifact SHA‑256 is a40e96e212ab87da251ac0d6dbb75bc543afa13438b5a6b9ebd073597ffdd820. The episode pass/fail oracle was deterministic_netops_validator_v5 (validator checks required final‑state constraints and workflow ordering) and produced binary episode scores used by the paired analysis executor. Analysis plan — The primary confirmatory test is an exact (two‑sided) McNemar test on paired binary outcomes with a paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729). The analysis produced the artifact bundle entry whose input_results_sha256 is given above (5337998d1d86...). For direct verification we cite the paired contingency artifact analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv (SHA‑256 c2ba9cdb5d0938eae910129ba511eadf309319e6e05b36d9e3b4860032deb80e) and the contamination summary analysis/contamination_summary.csv (SHA‑256 389227f0d1e81239c7498abd4944a04c59c92c5fa042b990e332796cd61c3222) which are archived with the execution bundle.

Primary estimand and inference: paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline = 0.0 percentage points; paired bootstrap 95% CI [0.0, 0.0] (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729); exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. Deterministic reconciliation — execution manifest and deterministic_reconciliation artifacts confirm complete pair accounting (complete_pair_count = 150) and no failed episodes. Representative per‑episode validator traces and the raw shared initial responses are archived in the execution bundle (representative examples are included in the manuscript evidence bundle).
sections.discussion: Interpreting a degenerate null — all 150 paired observations were concordant passes (n11 = 150); there were no discordant pairs (n10 = n01 = 0). In this degenerate configuration McNemar's test and the paired bootstrap produce numerically precise but vacuous inferential outputs (p = 1.0; CI collapsed) because no observed disagreements exist to attribute to the guarded intervention. The experiment therefore provides direct evidence that, under (i) the preregistered conservative detectors, (ii) the executed deterministic synthetic sample, and (iii) shared_initial_candidate generation semantics, the guarded procedure (which only acts when high‑confidence contamination is flagged) did not change validator outcomes for the sampled items. It does not imply absence of contamination in other benchmarks, real‑world corpora, other detectors, or other LLMs. Causes of the null outcome — two nonexclusive, artifact‑backed causes explain the degeneracy: (1) the executed items are provenance‑stable synthetic tasks (task_manifest entries use source_identifier values like "synthetic-netops:task-XXXXX" recorded in execution/task_manifest.jsonl; SHA‑256 b7c08599e3f96d8d5605a18f8f973e0707d7224327eeed7bde78c0d34cb83e55), which did not trigger preregistered high‑confidence detection heuristics; and (2) the preregistered shared_initial_candidate semantics (independent_condition_generation = false) produced identical model outputs across baseline and guarded episodes when no exclusions occurred, reducing sensitivity to generation‑level interventions. Design tradeoffs and operational implications — we followed preregistered choices to prioritize deterministic reproducibility and reduced model‑call variance; those choices made the audit conservative in the sense that it probed contamination flagging and downstream validator effects under tightly controlled, reproducible conditions. To bound contamination risk in broader practice, future audits should sample provenance‑rich, real‑world items, employ independent condition generation when testing generation‑level interventions, run multiple models, and include richer detectors plus human adjudication for borderline flags. Relation to preregistration → analysis mapping — the preregistration declared the primary confirmatory hypothesis label as H2; the archived analysis confirmatory record is reported under hypothesis_id 'H1' in the analysis input artifact (input_results_sha256 = 5337998d1d86aca507f77659d75cc9487cf3d87a157ed5044b8a9d5ff79b5586). We map analysis 'H1' to preregistered H2 here to preserve traceability and avoid identifier mismatch.
sections.conclusion: We executed a fully preregistered, artifact‑backed paired audit of conservative contamination detectors for LLM‑for‑NetOps evaluation. In the reproducible 150‑pair synthetic sample we observed zero preregistered high‑confidence contamination flags and identical validator pass rates (150/150 baseline, 150/150 guarded). The null outcome is artifact‑backed and arises from the executed sample composition (deterministic synthetic items) and the preregistered shared‑generation semantics; it does not generalize to public, web‑sourced benchmarks or other detectors/models. We correct the preregistration→analysis hypothesis identifier mapping, provide machine‑verifiable pointers to the primary analysis and contingency artifacts, and recommend stronger future audit designs (provenance‑rich sampling, independent generation, multi‑model scope, and mixed automated/manual adjudication).

limitations: Single‑model execution (gpt‑5‑mini) — results do not generalize across other LLM families, sizes, or training corpora.

Sampled items were provenance‑stable synthetic/deterministically generated tasks (source_identifier prefix "synthetic-netops:") for this run; absence of high‑confidence flags here may not reflect contamination prevalence in real‑world, web‑crawled benchmarks.

Generation semantics used shared_initial_candidate across baseline and guarded conditions (independent_condition_generation = false), producing identical model outputs when no exclusions occurred and thus limiting sensitivity to interventions that rely on independent re‑generation.

Contamination detection relied on preregistered conservative heuristics (exact match and fuzzy 5‑gram overlap thresholds); subtler contamination patterns (paraphrased memorization, partial leakage) may escape these heuristics and require richer provenance or manual adjudication.

Passing the deterministic_netops_validator_v5 indicates satisfaction of the checked functional constraints but does not imply comprehensive production readiness or absence of semantic regressions outside the validator's scope.
